units.name: app-core
units.role: The Flask application object: routing dispatch, request/response lifecycle, error handling, and the built-in development server.
units.description: This is the heart of the Flask web framework: the application object a developer creates with `Flask(__name__)`. It is split across two files for technical reasons (one holds the parts shared between synchronous and asynchronous Flask, the other adds synchronous-only behavior such as the built-in development server), but together they form a single class that a real web server calls for every incoming request. It matches the request to the right piece of application code, runs any 'before' and 'after' checks the developer registered, catches and reports errors, turns the code's return value into a proper web response, and, during local development only, can start its own small web server to listen on a socket. It must never assume there is only ever one request in flight at a time, and it must not silently swallow an unhandled error without reporting it.

units.name: scaffold
units.role: Shared base class both App and Blueprint inherit for registering routes, error handlers, request hooks, and resolving static/template locations.
units.description: This is the shared foundation both the main Flask application object and Blueprints are built on. It defines, in one place, how routes get registered, how error pages are hooked up, how code can run before and after each web request, and how an app or blueprint figures out where its 'static' and 'templates' folders live on disk. Neither Flask nor Blueprint reimplements this bookkeeping; they both inherit it from here, so behavior like registering a URL route works identically whether it is done on the whole app or on a smaller, reusable blueprint piece of it.

units.name: blueprint
units.role: A reusable, named group of routes, error handlers, and static/template assets that can be registered onto one or more apps later.
units.description: This is Flask's Blueprint feature: a way to package up a group of web pages, error handlers, and their associated static files/templates as a reusable, named bundle that isn't tied to any specific application. A developer builds a Blueprint the same way they'd build routes on the main app, then later registers it onto one or more real applications, optionally mounting it under a URL path prefix or a subdomain, and optionally nesting other blueprints inside it. It must never assume it is the only blueprint registered, or that it will only ever be registered once.

units.name: request-context
units.role: Tracks which application and request are currently active, and exposes the current_app/g/request/session proxies used from anywhere.
units.description: This unit is the piece of Flask that keeps track of 'what application and request are we currently inside of, right now'. When Flask starts handling a web request (or a developer manually opens a context using `with app.app_context()` in setup code, or `with app.test_request_context()` in tests), a context object is created holding the current app, the request data, and a per-request scratch space. That object is pushed onto a slot that is safe to use even with multiple simultaneous requests, and the rest of the framework and the developer's own code can then simply write `current_app`, `g`, `request`, or `session` from anywhere and transparently get the data for whichever request is presently running. When the request finishes, the context is popped and any registered cleanup functions run. It must never leak state from one request into another.

entrypoints.name: g

units.name: wrappers
units.role: Flask's own Request and Response classes, extending Werkzeug's with Flask-specific behavior.
units.description: This unit defines Flask's own versions of the request and response objects that every view function works with. Flask builds these as small extensions on top of Werkzeug's generic web request/response objects, adding Flask-specific conveniences: knowing which blueprint and URL endpoint matched a request, and wiring up which JSON library the request/response should use to parse or produce JSON bodies. Nearly every other unit in the framework refers to these two classes by type, making this a small but structurally central piece.

units.name: views
units.role: Class-based view dispatch (View, MethodView) as an alternative to plain view functions.
units.description: This unit lets a developer define a web page's behavior using a Python class instead of a plain function. Normally in Flask you write one function per URL; with this feature you can instead write a class, optionally with separate methods for GET, POST, DELETE, and so on, and Flask will automatically create the right function-like wrapper to plug into its routing system. It is a convenience layer on top of Flask's normal per-request handling, useful for building things like REST APIs where several HTTP methods act on the same resource.

units.name: helpers
units.role: General-purpose functions a view function calls while handling a request: URL building, redirects, flashing, sending files.
units.description: This unit provides the toolbox of everyday functions that a web page's Python code calls while handling a single visitor request: building a link to another page, sending the visitor elsewhere, bailing out with an error page, showing a one-time notification message, serving a file for download, shaping a custom response, and pulling a snippet out of a page template. It also has a couple of small support functions used only by the framework's own internals, such as finding where an app's code lives on disk. Almost every other unit depends on this one, but it depends on almost nothing itself.

units.description: This is the part of Flask that connects the application to the Jinja2 template engine. units.name: sessions
units.role: Signs and verifies the client-side session cookie, and defines the pluggable interface any session storage must follow.
units.description: This unit implements Flask's default way of remembering information about a visitor between web requests using a session cookie. It takes the small dictionary of data a page wants to remember, cryptographically signs it so it can't be tampered with by the browser or a malicious user, and packs it into a cookie sent to the visitor's browser. On the next request, it reads that cookie back, checks the signature is still valid and not expired, and hands the trusted data back to the rest of the application. It also defines the general contract any session storage mechanism must follow, so this default cookie-based approach could be swapped out for something else without changing the rest of the app. It must never trust a session value whose signature doesn't check out.

entrypoints.name: SessionInterface
entrypoints.plain: The contract any session storage backend must implement.

entrypoints.name: SecureCookieSessionInterface
entrypoints.plain: Flask's default session backend, using a signed cookie.

entrypoints.name: SessionMixin
entrypoints.plain: Marks a dict-like object as usable as a Flask session.

entrypoints.name: SessionInterface.open_session
entrypoints.plain: Reads and validates the session from an incoming request.

entrypoints.name: SessionInterface.save_session
entrypoints.plain: Writes the session back onto an outgoing response.

entrypoints.name: SessionInterface.make_null_session

effects.description: Cryptographically signs and verifies the session payload using itsdangerous.URLSafeTimedSerializer keyed on the app's secret key, to make the cookie tamper-evident (sessions.py:303-321,332,373).
Calls datetime.now(timezone.utc) to compute session cookie expiration (sessions.py:230).

units.name: json
units.role: JSON encoding/decoding for HTTP responses, plus a tagged-JSON format for packing extra types into the session cookie.
units.description: This unit handles converting Python data such as dictionaries, lists, dates, and IDs into JSON text for web responses and back again, and it lets a developer swap in a different JSON library if they want. It also has a special, separate tagged-JSON format that packs unusual Python values, like dates, UUIDs, byte strings, and tuples, into the signed cookie Flask uses to store session data, since plain JSON cannot represent those types on its own.

units.name: config
units.role: Application configuration storage, loadable from Python files, objects, environment variables, or JSON.
units.description: This unit manages application settings for a Flask web app. It provides a dictionary-like object that can be filled in with settings loaded from a Python file, a Python module or class, environment variables, a JSON file, or a plain dictionary. It also resolves relative file paths against the application's home directory, and offers a small helper that lets the main app object expose certain settings as regular attributes while actually storing them in this configuration dictionary.

units.name: cli
units.role: The `flask` command-line tool: app discovery, dotenv loading, the dev server, shell, and route listing.
units.description: This is the `flask` command-line tool. When someone types `flask run`, `flask shell`, or `flask routes` in a terminal, this code figures out which Flask application in the current project to use, optionally loads settings from .env/.flaskenv files, and then either starts a local development web server, opens an interactive Python shell pre-loaded with the app, or prints a table of the app's URL routes. It also gives application and extension authors a way to add their own custom commands to the `flask` tool.

units.description: This unit provides the tools Flask developers use to test their web applications without starting a real web server. It includes a fake browser that can send pretend web requests directly into the application in memory, and a fake command-line runner that can invoke `flask` CLI commands as if typed in a terminal, both for use inside automated test suites.

units.description: This part of Flask sets up how the application reports diagnostic messages, like errors and info notes, while it runs. It gives each Flask app its own named logger and, if the developer hasn't already configured logging themselves, quietly attaches a sensible default: messages get written either to the web server's designated error channel while a request is being handled, or to the program's standard error output otherwise.

units.name: debughelpers
units.role: Developer-facing diagnostics that make Flask's error output clearer when something is misconfigured, mainly in debug mode.
units.description: This unit provides friendlier error messages and warnings that only appear when a Flask application is running in debug mode. Instead of showing a developer a generic, confusing error, it explains likely misconfigurations in plain language, for example telling them a file upload field is missing because the HTML form forgot the right encoding, or listing every template loader that was tried and why none found a given template. It does no real work on its own; other units call into it at the moment something looks wrong so the resulting error is easier to understand.

units.description: This unit is a shared dictionary of type-hint names used throughout Flask's source code. Nearly every other unit imports this one to label its own function arguments and return types consistently.

units.name: signals
units.role: In-process event announcements (blinker signals) fired at key moments in a request's or app's lifecycle.
units.description: This is Flask's internal event system, used to announce that something notable has happened during the life of a request or application, such as a request starting, an exception occurring, or a template about to render. Other parts of Flask, and extensions written by developers, can subscribe to these announcements to run their own code at the right moment, without the core framework needing to know about them in advance. It must never be relied on for anything the application's normal control flow requires, since a signal may have no subscribers at all.

units.name: package-api
units.role: The published `flask` package namespace: decides which names from other units become `flask.X`.
units.description: This unit is the front door of the Flask package. It doesn't implement anything itself; it just decides, by importing and re-exporting, which classes and functions from every other unit become available when someone writes `import flask` and then reaches for `flask.something`. It must stay a thin, faithful list of what already exists elsewhere and never contain original logic of its own.

violations_observed.note: request-context is one of the most foundational units in the repo (nearly everything depends on it), yet it imports _CollectErrors from helpers for a small generic exception-collecting context manager used during teardown. The call does go through a listed entrypoint (helpers._CollectErrors), so this is not a boundary violation in the strict sense, but the dependency direction is backwards from a layering standpoint — _CollectErrors reads as infrastructure that request-context needs, not a view-facing helper. Recorded, not fixed.

violations_observed.location: src/flask/sansio/app.py (App.get_send_file_max_age, App.add_template_filter and related template_filter/global/test registration)
violations_observed.note: scaffold.py defines the shared route/hook registration machinery App and Blueprint both inherit, but get_send_file_max_age and the template_filter/template_global/template_test family are independently reimplemented in app-core (sansio/app.py) rather than living once in scaffold and being inherited. Both app-core and blueprint end up with their own near-duplicate copies. This is a design duplication inside otherwise-correct unit boundaries, not a case of one unit reaching into another's internals, so it is recorded here rather than treated as a partition error.
